Article Title: 'India's Got Latent' Gambit? Behind Vantika Agrawal's double bronze at Chess Olympiad | Exclusive
Article Text:
Vantika Agarwal opens up on Chess Olympiad and more

The one that got away

Vantika Agrawal (on right) during the game against China (Photo by Rafal Oleksiewicz for FIDE)

A team built for the challenges

Vantika Agrawal against US chess legend Irina Krush (FIDE Photo)

The IM looking to make a mark in elite circuit

Vantika Agrawal at Chess Olympiad (FIDE Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Life after the board, and 2027

NEW DELHI: The 46th edition of the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan's Samarkand, like usual, had just one rest day, after Round 6. Consequently, India's Vantika Agrawal, who had beaten US chess legend Irina Krush in that sixth-round matchup on Board 3, ended up with three days away from the board anyway — the scheduled rest day, plus two more rounds where she was kept off the lineup by captain Swayams Mishra , against Germany and Kazakhstan.Too much chess prep over those first two days had left Vantika looking for an escape on the third. Samay Raina's popular show 'India's Got Latent' came to her rescue. She binge-watched the latest episodes on her third day off, then returned to the board the next day and clinched a win over Uzbekistan's Nilufarkhon Imomkuzieva in her Round 9 matchup."Usually I don't watch that much, because you don't get the time. You prepare in the morning, then at night you're checking your opponent and discussing, then preparing again in the morning. By the afternoon you have a game, and you're tired. But this time, with the rest day plus two more days off, I had a lot of time, and I thought I'd practised so much chess already; let me relax a bit. So I watched some India's Got Latent episodes," she told TimesofIndia.com.Asked if she enjoyed it, there was no hesitation. "Yes, of course," she added. "I'd watched earlier episodes too, and then the new one there. It's nice. You just relax a bit."Vantika ended her campaign with a score of 6/8, five wins to her name, and an individual bronze medal in India women's bronze-clinching campaign. It's the quieter of India's two medal stories from this Olympiad, and arguably the more interesting one to hear told from the inside."I think it was good," she said of the experience overall. "I mean, of course, last time I won double gold. So this time also, we went for the gold, and it wasn't like we planned. We lost at the start to Poland. It wasn't as smooth as last year. But I'm glad that we won a lot of games and had a comeback, and managed to end on the podium; after a setback, we were able to come back and keep going. I think that was really important."If there's a single result Vantika would look back with some disappointment, it's the Round 10 draw against China that effectively ended India's gold-medal hopes. The 24-year-old lost her game to Lu Miaoyi on Board 3, with the team setting for a 2-2 draw."I was especially very upset about my game against China," the International Master (IM) admitted. "I think I was playing quite well, and after 40 moves it was very drawish. There were a lot of ways to make a draw. But somehow I was playing for a win at that moment. I knew my position wasn't better, but I decided to play for a win. Because of that, I made some foolish decisions."Part of the problem, she explained, was not knowing the full picture elsewhere. "At that moment it wasn't clear that we were winning on the fourth board, or I would have just gone for a draw. I was not sure what was happening on that board, and I thought I would play for a win," she recalled."Except for my loss against China, I think it was pretty good. Before that, I was on 5.5 out of 6. I had almost won all my games. If not for that loss, I would have even got an individual gold on board."I won against Krush. Then, after three days of rest, I won against an Uzbek player, also quite strong. So I think it was good, except one game I wasn't happy about."Shaking off a bad result, she said, came down to a fairly simple discipline as she added, "I think it was just to focus on the next game, and not really think about what had already happened."Vantika credited the dressing room, and Mishra specifically, for how the team absorbed the Poland loss and kept pushing."They all were very nice. Humpy (Koneru) was playing so well on board, Divya (Deshmukh), Savitha (Shri). Everyone was playing well. I think it can be seen that, in the end, we all won individual medals on our board," she remarked."We were kind of prepared for that, because last year also we lost to Poland and had that setback. So we were prepared that if something goes wrong, we will come together and fight as a team."That same candour extended to the one selection question hanging over the campaign, which was Vaishali Rameshbabu's dip in form, which saw her dropped for the final rounds."She is so strong she won the Candidates and is now the World Championship challenger. If she was in her full form, we would have easily crushed everyone. Those little chances that other teams got, like Poland, I don't think they would have got — we'd be winning on all boards," Vantika said.Asked whether the team dwells on these swings and misses while they're actually happening, Vantika was clear that they deliberately don't."I don't think we really think about that. Everyone tries to focus just on their own game, and our coach decides who plays, who doesn't, so that everything goes well. We don't think that much about these things," she added."Last time we had crushed everyone. We were 7 on 7, winning every game, not giving anyone a chance. This time it wasn't the same, even though we went with our best team. So the difficult part was accepting that every time you can't win gold, you can't crush everyone. It happens. That acceptance. That was difficult."When she was asked why she had been less visible on the elite circuit, Vantika Agrawal, already an Arjuna Awardee, was quick to push back on the perception that hers had been a quiet year outside the Olympiad bubble."I'm not invited to these top tournaments where the other girls, Humpy, Vaishali, Divya, are playing," she told this website. "But it's not that I'm not active. I'm playing a lot of open tournaments, and I'd say I'm more active than them. If you check my profile, I've played more games than any of them. It's just that I'm not playing in the tournaments everyone covers.""My rating is a bit low, and it's not easy to increase — even when I play very well, I gain maybe five or seven rating points. It's not easy to reach that level, and only once you reach it do you get invited to those tournaments," she further noted."This year I beat Song Yuxin; she played board two for China, in an open tournament. I beat Aditya Mittal too, who's over 2600 and hadn't lost a game all year before that — he just lost to me."There was a touch of frustration in how she recalled one particular near-miss for recognition."In the Tata Steel Rapid and Blitz in January, I tied for first place in Blitz, tied with Carissa Yip. But nobody covered that. It's just not being covered," she added with some disappointment.Whatever the coverage gap, Vantika insists it hasn't dented her own sense of where she stands and what she is aiming for — a Grandmaster (GM) title."I already feel confident, and I'm continuously working. It didn't change much after this Olympiad. I just want to focus on my goals and not think too much about all this," she added. "I'll continue playing more tournaments, trying to improve my skills and my level."Looking to 2027, her plan is a continuation rather than a reinvention. "I think I'll be doing the same thing, playing these open tournaments and trying to increase my rating, and see how it pans out," she admitted.ALSO READ: ‘Sometimes in chess, there are just these blind spots’: Nihal Sarin looks back at his Chess Olympiad loss to Uzbekistan | Exclusive Her studies, meanwhile, are largely settled. "I've completed my B.Com Honours. I was at SRCC College, Delhi University. After that, I've been focusing more on chess, because I had exams in December that clashed with tournaments I really wanted to play. Right now, I'm completely focused on chess, but I'll keep the option open; if I want, I'll do my Master's or an MBA."
Article Summary: Vantika Agrawal won an individual bronze medal in India women's bronze-clinching campaign. The 24-year-old lost her game to Lu Miaoyi on Board 3, with the team setting for a 2-2 draw. Vantika ended her campaign with a score of 6/8, five wins to her name.

Article Title: ‘Pakistan don’t offer much competition’: BCCI takes swipe after Asian Games final
Article Text:
India's team holds the national flag as they celebrate after winning the final T20I cricket match against Pakistan(PTI Photo)

Abhishek sets the tone, Tilak finishes strongly

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bowlers hold their nerve

BCCI president Mithun Manhas praised India’s handling of pressure in the Asian Games 2026 men’s cricket final against Pakistan , while taking a dig at the quality of competition offered by the arch-rivals in recent years.India secured one of their 21 gold medals at the Games after beating Pakistan by 19 runs in the final on Saturday, October 3, at the Korakuen Stadium in Nisshin, Japan. The closely fought contest saw Pakistan push India hard during the chase, but the defending champions held their nerve to retain the gold medal.Manhas, however, felt the result also highlighted what he believes is a decline in the competitiveness of India-Pakistan contests.“They defeated arch-rivals Pakistan, who I feel don't offer much competition anymore, and the way our team handled pressure situations... no other team in the world can do that," Manhas said after the final.The BCCI president also lauded India’s overall campaign, insisting that the team deserved its status as the tournament’s best side."By far the best team of the tournament. We are the defending champions, and the performance they have shown this time is commendable,” he added.Abhishek Sharma and Tilak Varma played key roles in India’s imposing total of 211, with both batters registering half-centuries.Manhas highlighted the contribution of the two batters and explained how India’s top and middle order combined to put Pakistan under pressure.“This is a team sport. Tilak Varma batted brilliantly, and Abhishek Sharma set the tone for the game. The job of openers is to build the innings, and the middle order finishes it. So, the openers basically set the tone," Manhas said.Abhishek gave India an explosive start, scoring 61 off 28 balls, while Tilak struck 51 off 22. India lost wickets during the middle overs but recovered through Tilak and Shivam Dube, who added 62 runs off 30 balls for the sixth wicket.“Team India's batting has been tremendous, and as for the bowling, I would say everyone contributed together to defend a good total,” the former Delhi batter added.India’s 211 was the first total above 200 in the tournament. Pakistan, though, mounted a serious challenge in the chase, led by Hasan Nawaz, who smashed 96 off 51 deliveries.India’s bowlers eventually managed to keep Pakistan to 182/6 after 20 overs, securing a 19-run victory. Axar Patel and Washington Sundar claimed two wickets each, while Jasprit Bumrah went wicketless but played a crucial role by bowling effectively during tense phases of the chase.The victory gave India back-to-back Asian Games cricket gold medals after their triumph in the previous edition.
Article Summary: India secured one of their 21 gold medals at the Games after beating Pakistan by 19 runs in the final on Saturday, October 3, at the Korakuen Stadium in Nisshin, Japan. The victory gave India back-to-back Asian Games cricket gold medals after their triumph in the previous edition.

Article Title: Ravichandran Smaran’s unbeaten 126 puts Rest of India in control against J&K in Irani Cup
Article Text:
Smaran Ravichandran(Special Arrangement)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In red-hot form, Ravichandran Smaran strengthened his case for higher honours with a fighting unbeaten 126 that put Rest of India in control against Jammu & Kashmir in the Irani Cup at the Sher-I-Kashmir Stadium on Saturday.The 23-year-old Karnataka left-hander, recently named his state’s captain for the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy season, struck 126 not out off 131 balls, with 15 fours and five sixes. It was his seventh first-class century in just his 20th match.RoI were in trouble at 197/8 on Day Three after Akash Deep fell for 1. Earlier, captain Rishabh Pant, who was unwell and walked in at No. 8, was trapped lbw by off-spinner Sahil Lotra for 8, while vice-captain Sarfaraz Khan fell for a rare five-ball duck, caught at slip off Umar Nazir.Smaran then took charge. He added an unbroken 109 for the ninth wicket with No. 10 Mukesh Choudhary, who battled for 47 balls for 9 not out. The stand may yet prove decisive, lifting RoI to 306/8 at stumps and extending their lead to 265.Having top-scored with 68 in the first innings, Smaran again showed the class that brought him 950 runs at 86.36 for Karnataka in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy. He reached his hundred off 113 balls and then smashed 26 off the next 18, attacking the J&K bowlers in fading light.J&K were left to rue repeated lapses. Their bowlers sent down 21 no-balls, with Umar Nazir alone overstepping 15 times in the innings and 22 times in the match. Nazir had Smaran given lbw on 104, with RoI at 237, but the no-ball buzzer saved the batter.Shubham Pundir also dropped a catch in the slips and appeared too deep for another regulation chance.Lotra was J&K’s best bowler, finishing the day with 3/71 in 26 overs.
Article Summary: RoI were in trouble at 197/8 on Day Three after Akash Deep fell for 1. Smaran added 109 for the ninth wicket with No. 10 Mukesh Choudhary, who battled for 47 balls for 9 not out. RoI to 306/8 at stumps and extend their lead to 265.

Article Title: Kumkum Mohod makes history with individual recurve gold, secures LA Olympics quota at Asian Games
Article Text:
India's Kumkum Anil Mohod (Image: REUTERS)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

OKAZAKI At the Asian Games , Kumkum Mohod has had very little to do with the world outside her competition. She has stayed off social media, had limited access to her phone and used it mainly to communicate with her parents.On Friday, she sent a picture of her medals to her father, Anil. His response was immediate: “There is a medal missing in this photo.” Typical of Indian fathers, he was reminding her of the task at hand.Like an obidient daughter then, the 17-year-old from Maharashtra completed the picture. On Saturday at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Gymnasium, she also wrote a slice of history that India — and South Korea — will remember for a long time. Kumkum became the first Indian to win an individual recurve archery gold at the Asian Games and, in the process, secured an Olympic quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Games.She finished her campaign with three medals: individual gold, women’s team gold and mixed team silver. Earlier, the trio of Ankita Bhakat, Kirti Sharma and Kumkum shattered South Korea’s dominance in the team event to claim their maiden gold.In the quarterfinals, Kumkum defeated Kang Chae-young 6-4.Kang, the 2025 individual world champion, was the favourite against an Indian prodigy who had qualified 10th. But Kumkum offered more than a glimpse of what was to come.In the semifinals, she swept aside China’s Jingyo Zhu 6-2.The final frontier was another Korean, Oh Ye-jin. And this time, Kumkum had to fight her way back.Oh took the opening set 29-27 and then moved 3-1 ahead. Kumkum responded with a perfect 30, only to follow it with consecutive 8s. Kumkum found her rhythm, produced a perfect 30 and forced the final into a shoot-off.One arrow now separated her from history. Oh shot an 8. Kumkum drew, aimed and released. A perfect 10.The shy 17-year-old had just done what no Indian recurve archer had done before at the Asian Games. A teenager who surprisingly enjoys listening to sad songs reserved those for the Koreans, for the Indians, she ensured there was only celebratory music.
Article Summary: Kumkum Mohod became the first Indian to win an individual recurve archery gold at the Asian Games. The 17-year-old secured an Olympic quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Games. She finished her campaign with three medals: individual gold, women’s team gold and mixed team silver.

Article Title: 'If Rory can win the Masters, so can you': Pranavi Urs overcomes triple bogey to script historic Asian Games gold
Article Text:
India's Pranavi Urs celebrates after winning the women's individual stroke play gold medal and women's team silver medal with Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar (REUTERS)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Overnight leader Pranavi Urs was channelling her inner Rory McIlroy as she negotiated the unsettling bumps that came with the pressure of the final day in the Asian Games women’s golf event.After she two-putted to golden glory on the rolling greens of Kasugai Country Club, she was a picture of calm, and quite unaware that she had sealed a historic first.Pranavi was in the zone. Only when playing partner Shannon Tan walked up to her, she realised her feat. “I thought it was to force a playoff,” she said. But it was the happy ending to an accomplished performance. It could also be a new beginning, instrumental in teeing off changes in the game back home.There was that gentle smile as she embraced her challengers. And then, she was ready for the customary soak by her friends Diksha Dagar and Aditi Ashok, with whom she shares team silver now. To go along with that shiny gold, thank you.“The first will always be the first. And I’ve always had that motto,” she said. “You are always going to have multiple winners, but you’re never going to have (another) first winner.”Last year, in a local ‘Battle of the Sexes’ battle on the IGPL circuit, the Mysuru golfer had emerged as the first woman to break through the barriers in a mixed field, beating boyfriend Karandeep Kochchar.“IGPL was good but gold beats it.”After playing in the howling wind and relentless rain on the Ayrshire links course of the Scottish Open, and leaving Las Vegas’ high-profile Aramco Championship with a creditable cut in a year she discovered new horizons, the 23-year-old Ladies European Tour (LET) golfer drew on all that mental fortitude in three sub-par rounds, and a fighting even-par final outing.With a three-stroke lead overnight, she admitted she and her anxious family, and boyfriend, couldn’t sleep in anticipation. “We all grew up in a joint family. Obviously, everyone couldn’t make it to Japan. My (cousin) sister Vidhatri, who also plays on the pro tour, was a nervous wreck. There’s always a live commentary going on in our group chats. And I told them, please record your reaction if I win. That was my last message before I teed off. ”It was the Bollywood-style denouement her mother Kaivalya wanted. “It was always my mom’s dream to have me represent the country and win, and then the national anthem. I’m glad I could do it in front of my parents. Dad (Sharath) cried, probably for the second time in his life. It’s funny because he cried when I was born. I did it for them.”It didn’t come easy. After a 66-63-66 push on the par-70 course, Pranavi stumbled with a triple bogey on the 3rd before India saw the sun rise, and former Major champ and six-time LPGA winner Ruoning Yin became the woman to chase. For viewers back home, it felt like a reprise of the disappointment of Aditi missing out on a medal at the Tokyo Olympics.But this was never meant to be a case of the ‘yips’. Only ‘yippee’, as Pranavi invoked the spirit of Rory, who won his first elusive Masters in 2025, having conceded a ‘triple’ early on. “I was thinking, if he can go and win the Masters, so can you. And I made three birdies after that,” was her reply to the doubters.When World No. 6 Yin’s birdie putt lipped out on the 18th, Pranavi arrived for her date with destiny.Next is a sweet homecoming for Urs, as she hunts for another first — a Ladies European Tour title — at the Hero Women’s Indian Open a little more than a fortnight from now. There, she will re-acquaint herself with Tan, the defending champion.As Pranavi ended a 24-year wait for a golf gold, Busan 2002 gold medallist Shiv Kapur found himself applauding Pranavi’s efforts. “I woke up early to follow the competition and was struck by her ability to remain composed under pressure,” he said. “I lived every moment. I hope the medals will be a huge boost for the game in India.” he added.
Article Summary: Pranavi Urs won the women's individual stroke play gold medal and women's team silver medal at the Asian Games. The 23-year-old Ladies European Tour (LET) golfer drew on all that mental fortitude in three sub-par rounds, and a fighting even-par final outing.

Article Title: India turn World Cup hurt into Asian Games gold, thrash Malaysia 5-1 to secure LA Olympics berth
Article Text:
Indian hockey team secure direct qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KAKAMIGAHARA: After the World Cup debacle, plenty was on the line at the Asian Games — places in the team, jobs and, most importantly, an Olympic berth.If the semifinal win over Pakistan was a narrow escape, the Indian men’s hockey team responded to its critics in style on a nippy Saturday night, defending its gold for the first time.India came with a plan and, despite Malaysia’s razor-sharp counter-attacks and man-to-man defence, backed its skill with timing and precision to run out 5-1 winners at the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium.It was one of the team’s most well-rounded performances in recent times.The occasion was special for Indian hockey. The men joined the women in securing qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics, completing a gold-medal double, another first for Indian hockey at the Asiad.The scoreline, however, did not tell the whole story. Malaysia were no pushovers. Both teams repeatedly took the aerial route to make inroads, though neither was able to establish sustained control.India broke the deadlock in the 11th minute when skipper Harmanpreet Singh ’s low drag-flick rocketed past goalkeeper Zaimi Deris Mat. Malaysia responded almost immediately. Veteran Shello Silverius collected an aerial pass from Faiz Jali on top of the circle and found the left corner with a superb finish.The Indian goalkeepers, Suraj Karkera and HS Mohith, who had faced criticism for their performances, stood up when it mattered. Amid midfield errors at both ends and chaotic attacking exchanges, Jugraj Singh unleashed a powerful drag-flick in the 23rd minute to restore India’s lead.But a one-goal advantage is never enough, especially with two quarters still to play. At the break, India regrouped. The hurt and humiliation of the World Cup remained fresh, and the players were determined not to let their chance at redemption slip away.“I think it was one of the most important achievements we can ever have because of what happened in the World Cup. It was tough to handle physically but, more importantly, it was mentally exhausting. We had been working very hard for a very long time. The World Cup did not pan out the way we wanted, and we couldn’t allow this to slip away,” Hardik Singh said.India eventually pulled away in the third quarter. Awarded a penalty stroke for an infringement, they converted through Hardik in the 42nd minute.Shilanand Lakra, arguably India’s best player on the night, then scored from close range before Harmanpreet put the finishing touches on the victory with three minutes remaining. The celebrations were muted. Relief, more than euphoria, was the overriding emotion.“We played a great game. We almost needed that semifinal to get into this mindset. I’m proud of the guys because of the first half’s performance from Malaysia, they really did make it difficult for us,” said chief coach Craig Fulton.There have been long waits, titles defended and medals lost at these Games. But amid it all, Indian hockey has produced one of its most heartwarming stories. With the job done in Japan, the focus now shifts to the LA Olympics.
Article Summary: Indian men's hockey team secure direct qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. India beat Malaysia 5-1 to complete a gold-medal double, another first for Indian hockey at the Asiad. Hardik Singh, Harmanpreet Singh and Shilanand Lakra scored for India.

Article Title: The Price of a Title Shot: When challengers had to pay to face the champion
Article Text:
Price of a title shot

When the Best Player Could Not Buy His Shot

Akiba Rubinstein

Lasker, Capablanca and a Battle Over Conditions

Emanuel Lasker (on the right) plays against José Raúl Capablanca

How the Champion–Challenger System Hit Its Limits

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

(Aarav Dengla is India’s 93rd Grandmaster. He is a keen observer and student of world history in general and

chess history

in particular.)

The upcoming world chess championship between defending champion D Gukesh of India and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan will take place in Geneva from November 22 to December 12. Organized under the aegis of FIDE, the match carries a prize fund of USD 2.5 million.The first world chess championship took place 140 years ago in the United States in 1886 between Wilhelm Steinitz (a Prague-born Austrian subject) and Johannes Zukertort (a British citizen). Played across three cities, the championship was contested for stakes totaling USD 4,000.What is interesting is how that USD 4,000 purse was assembled and how the match itself was organised. It was arranged under a private contract between the two contestants who had to agree to championship terms with each other. Each had to find backers willing to put USD 2,000 into the purse. Steinitz won by ten games to five, with five draws, in games played across New York, St. Louis and New Orleans.For its first six decades, the world championship was governed by bilateral contracts between the champion and the challenger, with the incumbent generally holding the stronger negotiating position.There was no fixed schedule. The champion decided whether to accept the challenge and on what conditions. The challenger had to find money from wealthy patrons or a club or another source.The system did not guarantee that the best player would have a shot at being the world champion.Akiba Rubinstein is considered to be among the best players of the early 1900s. Born in Poland, Rubinstein was introverted and fanatical about chess. Rubinstein reached his peak around 1912, winning five consecutive tournaments that year (San Sebastián, Pistyan, Breslau, Warsaw and Vilna). When he challenged Emanuel Lasker (then champion) in 1912, Lasker agreed to play on the condition that Rubinstein raised the money. Lasker’s financial demands were high, and Rubinstein struggled to meet them.Eventually, plans were made for a match in the autumn of 1914. Sadly, the match never happened, as World War I broke out in 1914, denying Rubinstein his shot at the world title. Just before Rubinstein challenged Lasker, José Raúl Capablanca sent a letter of challenge to Lasker in November 1911.At this point, Lasker had already held the title for seventeen years. Lasker responded to Capablanca’s challenge with a list of seventeen conditions which sparked a bitter dispute between the two. Among other conditions that Capablanca deemed unfair, Lasker demanded that the challenger win by a margin of at least 2 games, or Lasker would keep the title.The ensuing bitterness led to the two cutting off all communication. Negotiations resumed after the war, and the two signed an agreement in January 1920. However, in a dramatic twist in June 1920, Lasker resigned his world title in writing via a press announcement, declaring Capablanca his successor.Under a clause in their agreement, this made Capablanca champion, but the chess public was unwilling to accept a title handed over without a match. Lasker nevertheless agreed to play, while continuing to insist that Capablanca was already the champion. The world championship match finally happened in Havana, Cuba, in 1921 with a USD 20,000 purse, of which Lasker was guaranteed USD 11,000 and Capablanca USD 9,000 whatever the result. Capablanca dominated the contest and became the third World Chess Champion in 1921.Once champion, Capablanca proposed rules of his own in what came to be known as the London Rules. Under them, the champion could not be compelled to defend his title for a purse below USD 10,000. The champion received 20 percent as a fee, with the remaining 80 percent split 60:40 between the winner and the loser.This was a formidable sum in the 1920s. It took Alexander Alekhine almost five years to find financial support to challenge Capablanca. The Club Argentino de Ajedrez and Argentine supporters stepped in to put up the purse. This secured the official match in Buenos Aires, where Alekhine ultimately defeated Capablanca in 1927.Ironically, the London Rules stood in the way of Capablanca’s return as a challenger. Alekhine insisted that a rematch would have to follow the same rules. Talks dragged on for years without result, for reasons historians still dispute, and Capablanca died in 1942 without getting another shot at the title.This system of bilateral challenges ended in 1946 with the death of Alekhine. Alekhine still held the title at his death. There was nobody to challenge or negotiate with. FIDE, founded in 1924, stepped in.The Soviet Union joined FIDE in 1947, and in 1948 FIDE organised a world championship tournament. Five leading players took part, with Mikhail Botvinnik emerging as the winner and the new world champion. The subsequent qualifying cycle and tournaments were held under the aegis of FIDE with FIDE setting the rules.FIDE retained elements of the old structure. The champion still does not need to qualify and gets to defend the title. The challenger is determined through the cycle.Chess was hardly unique in using the champion–challenger model. Real tennis, the indoor game from which lawn tennis descends, claims the oldest world championship in any sport. Its first recorded champion, a Frenchman known only as Clergé, held the title in the 1740s, and it has always been decided by challenge. For long periods, the champion could accept or refuse a challenger, usually according to how much prize money the challenger’s sponsor offered, and several years could pass between matches.Professional boxing retained the champion–challenger structure but added sanctioning bodies to police it. A champion must periodically face a designated mandatory challenger or give up the belt. If the two camps cannot agree on terms, the sanctioning body holds a purse bid: promoters submit sealed offers, and the highest bidder stages the fight.Today, Sindarov does not have to find wealthy patrons or negotiate with Gukesh. He has already earned his seat across the board through a qualifying system. That may be the greatest difference between Geneva in 2026 and New York in 1886. The prize money has risen from thousands to millions, but the real progress is that a challenger no longer has to buy a shot at the title.
Article Summary: The first world chess championship took place 140 years ago in the United States in 1886. It was arranged under a private contract between the two contestants who had to agree to championship terms with each other. Each had to find backers willing to put USD 2,000 into the purse. The system did not guarantee that the best player would have a shot at being the world champion.

Article Title: 33 teams, no relegation, 198 matches: Mumbai football's Elite Division raises eyebrows
Article Text:
MFA Elite Division raises eyebrows

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MUMBAI: Mumbai’s top-flight football league is set to enter a season of unprecedented proportions, and not necessarily for the right reasons.The Mumbai Football Association’s (MFA) Elite Division, which kicks off on Oct 15, will feature 33 teams, a number virtually unheard of for a top division. What’s more, there will be no relegation for three years. At the end of that period, the division could have as many as 39 teams.The bloated league is the result of the MFA’s decision to merge its Private and Corporate leagues. The Corporate league had complained of being treated as a second-class competition, with poor scheduling and matches often confined to barely three months, making it difficult for companies such as Western Railway and Indian Navy to commit teams. Rather than address those concerns, the MFA opted for a merger.The 33 teams will be split into three groups of 11, with the top four from each advancing to a playoff stage comprising two groups of six. The top four will then enter the semifinals and final. In all, 198 matches will need to be staged.But venues and scheduling pose another concern. While the MFA is fighting to retain the Neville D’Souza ground, it has secured Cooperage for matches.At time slots of 10 am and 12 noon! When Mumbai’s heat and humidity are at their peak. AFC A-licensed coach Raj Shekar told TOI: “We must consider Mumbai’s heat and humidity and whether this is sustainable for players, clubs and spectators if we want to make the league popular.Shekar also questioned the 51.5% increase in the entry fee, saying it had, to his understanding, neither been approved by the president nor placed before the executive committee.Ex-India captain Godfrey Pereira was blunt: “It’s an absolute mess and definitely not something that should happen. How will it help grow the sport? Without relegation, what’s there to fight? The quality will deteriorate.”Sudhakar Rane, MFA secretary, told TOI that it’s the best they could do. “Teams in the corporate league were complaining, so we thought that this was the best solution. About the ground, these slots were the only ones available so there’s nothing we can do about it.”
Article Summary: Mumbai's top-flight football league is set to enter a season of unprecedented proportions. The Mumbai Football Association’s (MFA) Elite Division, which kicks off on Oct 15, will feature 33 teams. There will be no relegation for three years. At the end of that period, the division could have as many as 39 teams.

Article Title: 'I don’t want to resign': Litton Das rules out stepping down after Bangladesh’s Asian Games failure
Article Text:

Bangladesh captain Litton Das has ruled out stepping down from the leadership role despite his team’s disappointing Asian Games campaign, which ended without a medal.Bangladesh suffered a 63-run defeat to Sri Lanka in the bronze-medal playoff, marking the first time they have failed to win a cricket medal at the Asian Games. Sri Lanka, reduced to 21/4 early in their innings, were rescued by Tharindu Ratnayake, whose counter-attacking 65 turned the contest in his team’s favour.Litton admitted Bangladesh failed to perform at their best but credited Ratnayake for producing a match-changing innings.“I think we bowled very well in the first eight overs. Then you saw the kind of shots he played on this wicket. It was very difficult,” Litton told reporters after the match.“He batted extraordinarily and our bowlers had no clue how to come back. Credit has to be given to him for playing such an extraordinary innings. When we went out to bat, we couldn’t cover it up in any way. We were not up to the mark with the bat today,” he added.Litton, who scored just 2 and 0 in Bangladesh’s two matches at the Games, acknowledged that his own performance was below expectations. However, he insisted there was no reason for him to walk away from the captaincy.“My performance was not up to the mark. I could not perform well in both matches,” he said.“I don’t want to resign. There are ups and downs in cricket. One day it will be good and one day it will be bad. There is no point in resigning here. It’s normal. I came with a big target. When I can’t deliver that, everyone will feel bad, and that’s natural.“But as a team, we have given a lot in the past. I think we will give in the future too. We will try for that again,” Litton added.Reports of Bangladesh players leaving the team hotel without informing the authorities also emerged after the defeat, with the incident reportedly leading to the possibility of disciplinary action.Litton, however, defended the players and questioned the facilities available to the team, saying they needed suitable spaces to train as well as access to food that met their requirements.“Practice is required. Are there facilities there? No. So will a player be confined inside a room all day?” Litton said.“They need energy. If you think that the food being provided by the federation or the Asian Games is not suitable for us, then should a player not eat? If they want to eat, they have to go outside. That’s what the players did,” he added.
Article Summary: Bangladesh captain Litton Das has ruled out stepping down from the leadership role despite his team's disappointing Asian Games campaign. Bangladesh suffered a 63-run defeat to Sri Lanka in the bronze-medal playoff, marking the first time they have failed to win a cricket medal at the Asian Games.

Article Title: India withstand Hasan Nawaz onslaught to beat Pakistan, win Asian Games gold
Article Text:
India beat Pakistan by 19 runs in the Asian Games men’s T20 final to claim gold after posting 211/6 and restricting Pakistan to 192. (Image: Reuters)

TimesofIndia in

Aichi-Nagoya

:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Brief scores: India 211-6 (A Sharma 61, Tilak Varma 51 not out, Shivam Dube 27; Arafat Minhas 2-25, Ahmed Daniyal 2-43) beat Pakistan 192-6 in 20 overs (Hasan Nawaz 96, Saim Ayub 29; Axar Patel 2-29, Washington Sundar 2-29) by 19 runs.

The warm hugs, high-fives and handshakes that have become a norm between Indian and Pakistani athletes across sports at the Asian Games took a leave of absence when the cricket teams played at the Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin on Saturday.Enter Shreyas Iyer and his men. There were no customary courtesies, only an expression of rivalry and an unmistakable desire to win gold. By the time the sun set over the Owari Hills, the gold medal was glistening around the necks of Iyer and his men. But Pakistan had ensured it was no procession, launching a late fightback that put the champagne on ice for the defending champions.Opting to bat, India rode on half-centuries from Abhishek Sharma (61; 28b, 3x4, 7x6) and Tilak Varma (51*; 22b, 2x4, 4x6) to post 211/6. Pakistan, reduced to 31/3 at the end of the Powerplay, appeared headed for a heavy defeat. Then Hasan Nawaz took charge, smashing a breathtaking 51-ball 96 (5x4, 7x6). But his assault came too late as Pakistan finished on 192/6, handing India a 19-run victory.On a surface that played differently from the one used in the semifinals, India’s openers took a little time to settle in. Pakistan’s decision to open with off-spinner Saim Ayub looked like a good move but the bubble burst soon after as Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Abhishek soon found their range.Sooryavanshi provided the early fireworks, dropping to one knee to launch leg-spinner Saad Masood over the bowler’s head before pulling the next delivery through midwicket. Abhishek was not to be outdone, finding the region beyond mid-on.While Sooryavanshi and Sanju Samson returned to the makeshift dressing room, Abhishek, who survived a dropped catch and a run-out, tormented the Pakistan attack as India raced to 81 in the Powerplay.Length was a major issue for Pakistan, who repeatedly bowled short to the in-form batters. Once they got that right, there was a lull of almost six overs without a boundary before Tilak and Shivam Dube launched the late assault.The final push came in the penultimate over, which yielded 23 runs and propelled India beyond 200.With Pakistan 31/3 after six overs, an early finish seemed on the cards. Hasan Nawaz had other ideas. The right-hander produced an innings to remember, keeping Pakistan in the contest almost single-handedly. But by then, India had done enough to ensure the gold stayed with them.For Iyer, the victory was also a reward for a team that had refused to let circumstances derail its campaign.“Ecstatic,” was how he described the feeling. “Since the day we arrived in Japan, it was raining cats and dogs and we couldn’t practise for almost a week. But the boys prepped themselves and we trained on the side. We didn’t complain, we didn’t give any reason,” Iyer said. “That was a sign of a champion team and today was just a reflection of that,” he added.Head coach VVS Laxman said the Asian Games gold carried a special significance for players who had already experienced World Cup success.With cricket returning to the Olympics in 2028, Randy Newman’s super hit song ‘I Love LA’ may well be playing in the players’ mind.
Article Summary: India beat Pakistan by 19 runs in the Asian Games men’s T20 final to claim gold. India rode on half-centuries from Abhishek Sharma (61) and Tilak Varma (51*) to post 211/6. Pakistan, reduced to 31/3 at the end of the Powerplay, appeared headed for a heavy defeat. Hasan Nawaz took charge, smashing a breathtaking 96 (5x4, 7x6) But his assault came too late as Pakistan finished on 192/6, handing India a 19-run victory.

Article Title: India vs West Indies ODI series rewrites record books with highest scoring rate ever
Article Text:
West Indies captain Shai Hope and Gudakesh Motie celebrate (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The India-West Indies ODI series was a run-fest from start to finish, with the three-match contest setting a new record for the highest scoring rate in a bilateral series involving at least three ODIs.The series recorded a scoring rate of 7.43 runs per over, the highest in the format for a bilateral series of three or more matches.The previous record was held by England's 2015 home series against New Zealand, which produced a scoring rate of 7.15 runs per over. India themselves were involved in the third-highest mark, scoring at 7.00 runs per over against England in the 2017 series. England's 2019 series against Pakistan comes fourth at 6.97.The numbers underline just how explosive the India-West Indies contest was.The first ODI saw 595 runs scored, with West Indies making 295 for seven before India chased down the target in just 41.4 overs, finishing on 300 for two.The second ODI raised the bar considerably. West Indies piled up 405 for seven, only for India to chase down the target in 43.3 overs, reaching 406 for two. The match produced 811 runs.The run-scoring continued in the series finale, with India making 351 for seven before West Indies completed a record chase of 352 for five in 48.2 overs.The third ODI alone produced 703 runs.Across the three matches, both teams repeatedly crossed the 300-run mark. India eventually won the series 2-1, sealing victories by eight wickets in the first two matches before West Indies produced a five-wicket consolation win in the finale.The series was so heavily tilted towards the batters that, apart from Kuldeep Yadav's four-wicket spell in the opening ODI, there was little in the bowling departments to remember. The India spinner's spell stood out as one of the few occasions when a bowler managed to exert sustained influence on a contest otherwise dominated by the bat.Even India's 406-run chase in the second ODI prompted head coach Gautam Gambhir to question whether such batting-friendly conditions offered enough preparation for the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.Gambhir was unequivocal in his assessment after the match."There has to be a bit more contest between bat and ball because this is not cricket, this is only batting," he said.His comments pointed to a larger concern for India despite their 2-1 series win. While the extraordinary scoring rates made for compelling batting numbers, the series also exposed questions around India's bowling attack.Kuldeep was the notable exception, with his four-wicket haul in the first ODI providing one of the few standout bowling performances of the series. Beyond him, India struggled to consistently make an impact with the ball across the three matches.Jasprit Bumrah and Axar Patel are expected to return to the ODI setup, which should strengthen the attack, but the series has nevertheless left India with questions over the depth and balance of their bowling options ahead of the 2027 World Cup.
Article Summary: The India-West Indies ODI series set a new record for the highest scoring rate in a bilateral series involving at least three ODIs. The series recorded a scoring rate of 7.43 runs per over. The previous record was held by England's 2015 home series against New Zealand.

Article Title: Shai Hope battles cramps as West Indies chase down 352 to register five-wicket win over India in third ODI
Article Text:
West Indies' Shai Hope plays a shot during the third and final One Day International (ODI) cricket match of a series between India and West Indies, in Mullanpur. (PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New Chandigarh: India’s ODI team is in a phase where it is on the lookout for stern challenges to identify its own core group for the World Cup in South Africa, which is a year away. After two lopsided victories in the first two ODIs, India were finally tested by West Indies for the entire length of the match, which ended with captain Shai Hope’s effortless unbeaten 162 off 143 balls chasing down 352-run target with 10 balls and five wickets remaining.Coming out to open the batting, Hope overshadowed KL Rahul’s counterattacking unbeaten 129 off 87 balls that propelled India to 351/7. Dew may have played a part, but Hope’s experience tamed down India’s inexperienced bowling with consummate ease as the West Indies team pulled one back in the series to soothe the pain of the impending pay cuts in their match fees.India’s greatest challenge coming into the series was to identify a backup pace attack to complement Jasprit Bumrah. The team management may have to wait a little longer to nail the pace attack.Be it the pace and movement up front in the match or Hope’s unwavering temperament in the chase, India were always playing catch-up. When Jayden Seales breached Virat Kohli’s defence immediately after removing Shubman Gill off the previous ball in the third over of the match, the conditions seemed like what one may expect in South Africa in a year’s time. If ever the selectors needed an affirmation about Rohit Sharma’s capability to survive and dominate in testing conditions, his carefully paced knock of 92 off 85 to put India back on track did just that.After the first 10 overs of the match, where India laboured to 32/2, Rohit broke free along with Ruturaj Gaikwad to resume the usual business of brisk run-scoring. India kept losing wickets at regular intervals, but the scoring rate maintained an upward trajectory till they finished with 351/7.As has been the trend in the series, run scoring never looked challenging for the batters. Just like India cruised to victory while chasing big totals in the previous two games, West Indies batters too looked fairly untroubled in the evening. The only thing that troubled Hope was running between the wickets with cramps. Had Amir Jangoo not been run out for 67 off 56, things would have moved at a faster rate for West Indies.Rahul’s innings did have a couple of dropped catches in it, but his fluency was such that one couldn’t make out this was his only outing with the bat in the series. Rahul faces stiff competition from Ishan Kishan for holding on to his spot in the XI. Saturday’s knock will improve his stocks as the lead wicketkeeper in the team.
Article Summary: West Indies captain Shai Hope’s effortless unbeaten 162 off 143 balls chased down 352-run target with 10 balls and five wickets remaining. Hope overshadowed KL Rahul's counterattacking unbeaten 129 off 87 balls that propelled India to 351/7. India were always playing catch-up.

India signed off from the Asian Games 2026 in fourth place with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. The final tally was below the record 106 medals won at Hangzhou, but a strong finish in the final days changed the complexion of the campaign.From Kumkum Mohod’s historic archery gold and Aman Sehrawat’s wrestling triumph to disappointing campaigns in tennis and some traditionally strong disciplines, India’s Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games journey had its share of soaring highs and hard misses.Here are India's biggest hits and flops from Aichi-Nagoya.Archery was arguably India's biggest success story when it came to gold medals.India won five gold medals, with the women's and men's compound teams, mixed compound team, women's recurve team and Kumkum Mohod's individual recurve triumph providing the highlights.The biggest moment came from 17-year-old Kumkum Mohod, who became the first Indian woman to win an individual recurve gold at the Asian Games.Her success, along with the women's recurve team's gold, gave Indian archery a memorable Games. Kumkum also added a silver in the mixed recurve team event with Dhiraj Bommadevara.Indian hockey delivered when it mattered most.The women's team ended a 44-year wait for an Asian Games gold, while Harmanpreet Singh's men's team defeated Malaysia 5-1 in the final to retain the title.The two victories also had an Olympic dimension, with India's performances securing qualification opportunities for Los Angeles 2028.The men's final was the perfect way to close India's medal campaign, with the 5-1 victory delivering the country's 21st gold.India's cricket teams delivered two more gold medals.The women's team retained its title, while the men's side defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final to successfully defend India's Asian Games crown. Abhishek Sharma's explosive batting and Tilak Varma's unbeaten 51 were among the highlights of the men's final.The men's final also became one of the most talked-about sporting moments of the Games, thanks to the India-Pakistan rivalry.India's boxers produced one of the strongest late surges of the Games, winning three gold medals.Lovlina Borgohain, Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal emerged as champions in their respective categories.For Lovlina, the victory was particularly significant: she became only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to win an Asian Games boxing gold.Aman Sehrawat's gold was one of the more compelling individual stories of the Games.The wrestler had endured a difficult period involving illness, absences and a loss of motivation following the Paris Olympics. His return to the top at Aichi-Nagoya turned the campaign into a personal comeback story as well as a medal-winning one.India finished with two wrestling golds, along with silver and bronze medals.Pranavi Urs created history by winning India's first women's individual golf gold at the Asian Games.India also took silver in the women's team event, making golf one of the country's notable success stories in Aichi-Nagoya.Kabaddi remained one of India's most dependable gold-medal sports at Aichi-Nagoya.Both the men's and women's teams won gold, allowing India to retain its titles and reinforce its dominance in the sport at the Asian Games.The double triumph was another strong performance from a discipline where India continues to set the continental benchmark.Athletics was India's biggest contributor by overall medal count, producing 24 medals.The medal haul included silver medals for Ancy Sojan, Sarvesh Kushare, Sawan Berwal, Gulveer Singh and others, along with multiple bronze medals across track and field.The sport also produced historic moments, including Baranica Elangovan's first-ever Asian Games pole-vault medal for India and Vithya Ramraj's national-record bronze in the 400m hurdles.The caveat is the gold count. Athletics produced a huge volume of medals but only one gold, meaning the sport's conversion into top-of-the-podium finishes remains an area India will want to improve.Tennis was arguably India's biggest disappointment.For the first time in four decades, India failed to win a single Asian Games tennis medal. The campaign ended without a podium finish despite the country's historically strong record in the sport at the continental event.The result was particularly striking because tennis has traditionally been one of India's reliable Asian Games medal sports.Shooting eventually contributed 15 medals, including three golds, making it one of India's biggest medal-producing sports.But the campaign began with considerable disappointment.India endured several fourth-place finishes and missed opportunities before Suruchi Singh and Kamaljeet finally ended the wait for a shooting gold.Tilottama Sen and Vidarsa Vinod, for example, finished fourth and fifth respectively in the women's 50m rifle 3P individual final.The final medal count was impressive, but expectations around India's shooters were even higher.Badminton managed only one medal — a bronze in the men's team event.The result was underwhelming for a sport that has produced some of India's biggest Asian Games and Olympic stars.The campaign was also overshadowed by criticism of the Games' scheduling and organisation. H.S. Prannoy, who won the men's team bronze, described the experience as “sad” for athletes and criticised the accommodation and scheduling arrangements.Equestrian was another discipline that failed to make a mark for India at Aichi-Nagoya.Despite India's pedigree in the sport and its strong performances at previous Asian Games, the contingent returned without a medal.The result added to a list of disciplines where India was unable to convert participation and experience into podium finishes, making equestrian a relatively disappointing campaign.Several disciplines failed to make a significant impact for India at the Asian Games 2026. Esports was among the clearest disappointments, with India failing to win a medal across its events, while fencing and volleyball also ended without a podium finish despite sizeable contingents and expectations.Table tennis managed only one bronze, a modest return for a sport with India’s growing international stature, making it another underwhelming campaign.Rowing produced a solitary bronze, leaving the discipline with a relatively limited medal haul. Taken together, these results highlight the gaps India still needs to address beyond its stronger medal-producing sports.
Article Summary: India signed off from the Asian Games 2026 in fourth place with 85 medals — 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. India won five gold medals, with the women's and men's compound teams, mixed compound team and Kumkum Mohod's individual recurve triumph providing the highlights. India's cricket teams delivered two more gold medals.

Article Title: ‘I have only one life’: How 3 Idiots inspired Bobby Kumar's Asian Games journey
Article Text:
Bobby Kumar (right) with Akash Yumnam after winning bronze at Asian Games and (pic right) with his father Dharmendar Upadhyay

Kolkata:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

When Bihar’s Bobby Kumar watched the Bollywood blockbuster 3 Idiots, one message stayed with him: follow your passion.Growing up in a state where academics often take precedence over sport, Bobby found himself caught between expectations and his love for playing games. Inspired by the film’s message of pursuing what truly makes one happy, he chose a different path.Today, that decision has earned him an Asian Games bronze medal in sepak takraw as part of the Indian men’s quadrant team that reached the semifinals before losing to hosts Japan in Nagoya.“I have only one life. I didn’t want to spend it thinking only about studies,” Bobby recalled from Nagoya. “The message of 3 Idiots stayed with me. It made me feel that I should follow my heart and do what I truly enjoy.”Before discovering sepak takraw, Bobby played cricket in Patna. Like many families in Bihar, his parents, Manju Devi and Dharmendar Upadhyay, initially wanted him to focus on education and build a secure future. He tried, but sport proved impossible to ignore.“Whenever I saw other children playing, I wanted to play too. Gradually, I started enjoying it more and more and decided that I wanted to pursue sport seriously,” he said.It wasn’t cricket that eventually became his calling. Inspired by his elder brother Sunny, Bobby took up sepak takraw in 2014-15 and began training under coach Pankaj Kumar and Karunesh Kumar at a nearby park in Kankarbagh.“I could see his potential from the very beginning. He was disciplined, hardworking and eager to learn. That’s why I always believed he could achieve something special,” said Pankaj, who has been coaching since 2002.Bobby’s rise was steady and he completely committed himself to the sport in 2019 when he joined the Sports Authority of India (SAI) training centre in Bareilly, Uttar Pradesh.The road to the Asian Games, however, was far from smooth. Bobby was in contention for the previous edition but missed out after changes to the squad. Rather than letting the setback define him, he turned it into motivation.“I made the 2026 Asian Games my target. I wanted to make sure I was in the main squad and not just among the reserves,” he said. “I was so focused on that goal that I even included ‘2026’ in my passwords as a daily reminder.”That focus was tested by personal challenges. Yet, with support from teammates, particularly Akash Yumnam, Bobby managed to remain fully focused on the competition.India battled through a difficult group featuring powerhouses Myanmar and Vietnam before eventually securing bronze. For Bobby’s father, the medal was the reward for years of dedication.“I couldn’t be prouder of Bobby. He has always been passionate about sports. Even when he was studying at Kendriya Vidyalaya, he used to win medals in skipping events. Today, people recognise me because of what he has achieved. Everything he has earned has come through his hard work and commitment,” said Dharmendar, who also has a daughter named Isha Kumari.As for Pankaj, the achievement is equally satisfying.“Seeing him win an Asian Games medal is a matter of immense pride. As a coach, you always hope your students reach the biggest stage, and Bobby has done that,” he said.And if the coach’s assessment is accurate, the Asian Games bronze may only be the start. “Bihar is now among the strongest states in the country in this sport. We have several players competing at the national level, and Bobby’s medal will inspire many more youngsters to take it up,” Pankaj added.
Article Summary: Bobby Kumar won a bronze medal in sepak takraw at the Asian Games. He was part of the Indian men’s quadrant team that reached the semifinals before losing to hosts Japan in Nagoya. His father Dharmendar Upadhyay said the medal was the reward for years of dedication.

Article Title: Harmanpreet Singh leads the charge as India tear through Malaysia 5-1 for Asian Games men's hockey gold; seal LA28 Olympics spot
Article Text:
India's players celebrate a goal during the men's Hockey final's gold medal match between Malaysia and India in the ongoing 20th Asian Games, in Gifu, Japan.

The Indian men's hockey team defended their Asian Games gold medal and secured a spot at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics after defeating Malaysia 5-1 in the final in Kakamigahara, Japan, on Saturday.India had never won successive Asian Games gold medals, making Saturday's final an opportunity to create history. Harmanpreet Singh-led India made the most of it as they successfully defended their title.Malaysia secured the silver, while Pakistan won the bronze by defeating South Korea 5-3 earlier in the day.India started slowly as Malaysia, as expected, defended in a low block and managed to keep the Indian attack out despite the pressure. India eventually broke the deadlock in the 12th minute through Harmanpreet.India won their first penalty corner after Hardik played Abhishek into the circle and the forward found a Malaysian defender's foot. Harmanpreet took the first attempt, but the push from Hardik was poor. India, however, won another penalty corner.Harmanpreet made no mistake with his second chance. The trap was better this time and he beat the first rusher with his drag-flick before sending a powerful shot past the goalkeeper, who could not see it to put India in the lead.Malaysia responded quickly and equalised just two minutes later in the 14th minute. Shello Silverius thrashed a half volley into the roof of the net from the left end of the circle. He received an aerial ball from the right and got his shot away almost immediately.The first quarter ended 1-1.India regained the lead in the 23rd minute through another penalty corner. Shilanand Lakra received the ball on the left wing and found a chance to enter the circle, but the attack was stopped. Soon after, Lakra made another run into the circle and this time won a foul.Jugraj Singh converted the penalty corner to put India 2-1 ahead.Malaysia continued to press India and put the defending champions under pressure, but India held on to their lead at half-time.India extended their advantage in the 42nd minute when Hardik Singh scored from another penalty corner. The goalkeeper moved to his right early, allowing Hardik to place the ball centrally and make it 3-1 for India.India exerted their dominance in the last few minutes as Abhishek scored another goal for India in the 55th minute to make it 4-1. Harmanpreet followed soon after to score his second goal of the match through penalty corner with a rocket drag-flick flying into the top left of the goal to put India into a comfortable 5-1 lead.India held on to complete a 5-1 victory over Malaysia and successfully defend their Asian Games title. The triumph came a day after the Indian women's hockey team also won gold, beating China 1-0 in the final, giving India a golden double in hockey.
Article Summary: India had never won successive Asian Games gold medals, making Saturday's final an opportunity to create history. Harmanpreet Singh-led India made the most of it as they successfully defended their title. Malaysia secured the silver, while Pakistan won the bronze by defeating South Korea 5-3 earlier in the day.

Article Title: Screensaver turns real: Aman Sehrawat’s gold on phone now around his neck
Article Text:
Aman Sehrawat

NEW DELHI: For months, Aman Sehrawat had carried a picture of the Asian Games gold medal on his phone. It was more than a wallpaper; it was a daily reminder of the colour he wanted after returning from Hangzhou with bronze. On Saturday, after beating North Korea’s reigning world champion Han Chong Song 11-7 in the 57kg final, Sehrawat looked at the real medal, bit it, and allowed himself a moment of disbelief. The picture had become reality.The road to it had not been smooth. A cut beneath his left eye left him bruised during the bout, but not distracted. Han surged back from 1-6 to lead 7-6, yet Sehrawat answered with two takedowns, regained control and closed out the comeback. Earlier, he had beaten Japan’s Yamato Ogawa 20-9, Kazakhstan’s Nurdanat Aitanov 12-1 and Tajikistan’s Aiaal Belolyubskii 14-8.The gold also carries a difficult lesson. Last year, Sehrawat was eliminated from the World Championships after weighing 1.7kg over the 57kg limit, which led to a one-year suspension from the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI). The ban was later lifted after he apologised. He competed at 61kg in the Zagreb Open and Asian Championships, taking silver at both, before returning to 57kg and winning the Budapest Ranking Series event ahead of the Games.Weight had become a difficult proportion to manage, but that discipline made Saturday sweeter. Sehrawat, now 23, is already a U-23 world champion, a Paris Olympic bronze medallist and a Hangzhou bronze medallist. Now he has added the continental crown and upgraded his Asian Games colour from bronze to gold.Sehrawat’s wrestling journey began in far darker circumstances. He lost his mother at 10 and his father a year later, leaving him orphaned at 11. His maternal uncles stepped in, brought him to Delhi’s Chhatrasal Stadium and set him on a path from grief to purpose. Under coach Lalit Kumar, the boy from Haryana became a solid wrestler with a force to reckon with.India’s remarkable wrestling campaign at the ongoing edition became even sweeter, and historic as well, after Antim Panghal’s silver in women's 53kg and Deepak Punia’s bronze in men's 97kg took the nation's tally to six wrestling medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze. It was the country’s best Asian Games haul in 64 years. The last time India collected more was Jakarta in 1962, with 12 medals.Antim, a Hangzhou bronze medallist, reached the final of her weight division hoping to become only the second Indian woman after Vinesh Phogat to win Asian Games wrestling gold. Japan’s Moe Kiyooka, however, proved too sharp, controlling the contest and winning 9-1. Antim’s silver still underlined a strong campaign, though gold remained beyond reach.Punia added bronze after edging Mongolia’s Gankhuyag Ganbaatar 2-1 in the medal-deciding repechage bout. He had beaten China’s Zhou Junpeng 12-2 before a quarterfinal walkover, then lost an 8-9 semifinal to Uzbekistan’s Sherzod Poyonov. He recovered to finish on the podium.For Indian wrestling, Nagoya ended with an impressive haul. For Sehrawat, it ended with something more personal: a wallpaper, a promise and, finally, the gold he had spent months imagining.
Article Summary: Aman Sehrawat wins gold in men's 57kg at the Asian Games. He beat reigning world champion Han Chong Song 11-7 in the final. India's haul of six wrestling medals was the country's best in 64 years. Antim Panghal won silver in women's 53kg and Deepak Punia bronze.

Malaysia's only goal came from Shello Silverius in the 14th minute.Harmanpreet finished as the tournament's top scorer with 12 goals. India also earned 14 penalty corners compared to Malaysia's two.The victory gave India their fifth Asian Games men's hockey gold, after previous triumphs in 1966, 1998, 2014 and 2022. India also became only the second country after Pakistan to win back-to-back Asian Games men's hockey golds.Harmanpreet became the first Indian men's hockey captain to lead the team to two Asian Games gold medals.The triumph came a day after the women's team beat defending champions China 1-0 to win their first Asian Games gold in 44 years and secure an Olympic berth.It was the first time that both Indian hockey teams finished on top of the podium at the same Asian Games.Aman Sehrawat upgraded his bronze from the 2023 Hangzhou Games to gold by beating North Korea's reigning world champion Chong Song Han 10-7 in the men's 57kg final.The 23-year-old was initially frustrated by Han's defensive approach but took control after being put on the clock. He built a 6-1 lead before Han fought back to move 7-6 ahead.Aman responded with two more takedowns to seal the gold.It was India's second wrestling gold of the Games after Sujeet Kalkal's title on Friday.Antim Panghal, meanwhile, had to settle for silver after losing 1-9 to Japan's 2024 world champion Mei Miyooka in the women's 53kg final.Antim could not find a way through Miyooka's defence and attack.Deepak Punia added a bronze in the men's 97kg category after beating Mongolia's Gankhuyang Ganbataar 2-1.India finished the wrestling competition with six medals — two gold, two silver and two bronze.India retained their Asian Games men's T20 cricket title after beating Pakistan by 19 runs in the final.Abhishek Sharma smashed 61 off 28 balls, hitting seven sixes, while Tilak Varma produced an unbeaten 51 off 22 balls as India posted 211/6.Pakistan fought back through Hasan Nawaz, who scored 96 off 51 balls, but India held their nerve to restrict them to 192/6.The victory also extended India's head-to-head dominance over Pakistan to 6-0 since the start of the 2024 T20 World Cup.Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an individual Asian Games golf gold.The 23-year-old held her nerve despite a triple bogey on the third hole and recovered with three birdies to finish the final round at even-par 70.She finished at 15-under 265, one stroke ahead of China's Yin Ruoning.Pranavi's gold also helped India win the women's team silver, with Aditi Ashok and Diksha Dagar completing the team.It rounded off India's best Asian Games golf performance in 44 years.Teenager Kumkum Mohod produced another landmark performance by winning India's first-ever Asian Games individual women's recurve gold.Kumkum beat South Korea's Oh Yejin 6-5 in a shoot-out, finding the 10-ring with her final arrow to clinch the title.Her run to the final also secured an individual quota place for India at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The quota belongs to India, while the final selection of the athlete will be decided through the federation's trials.Neeraj Chauhan completed a memorable day for Indian recurve archery by beating compatriot Dhiraj Bommadevara 6-4 for the men's individual bronze.Neeraj fought back from 2-4 down before winning the deciding set.He became only the second Indian male archer after Tarundeep Rai to win an individual recurve medal at the Asian Games.
Article Summary: India's medal tally now stands at 85 medals - 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze. Captain Harmanpreet Singh led from the front as India beat Malaysia 5-1 to win the men's hockey gold. Abhishek Sharma smashed 61 off 28 balls, hitting seven sixes, as India retained their Asian Games men's T20 cricket title.

Article Title: Estevao, Pedro and Samuel Lino expose India’s shortcomings as Brazil cruise to 4-0 victory in Kolkata
Article Text:
Brazil have it easy against India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: Brazil 4 and India 0. The staggering gap between the five-time world champions and the one with 137 Fifa ranking and hardly any international pedigree of late looked too obvious to mention.If goalkeeper Gurpreet Singh Sandhu was partially responsible for allowing Brazil to go 2-0 up in the first half, with Estevao and Pedro finding the target in 28 and 42 minutes, Samuel Lino’s brace as a second-half substitute, in 58 and 90+5 minutes, were quite pleasing to the eye. The result was unapologetically direct. This was also a reminder that when the game as a contest melted into a foregone conclusiona, the line between reverie and reality got blurred and the gap in class and quality between the two sides looked as large as the geographical distance between the countries.In Brazil’s rebuilding process, this match perhaps lacked the usual significance and substance and was more about paying homage to their massive fan base in this part of the world. In India’s transitional phase, this didn’t even come with its conventional contour of something to fight for but rather as an eerily abstract way of negotiating a challenge they didn’t have the wherewithal to survive, let alone rescuing anything from it.Yet, despite odds heavily stacked against them, India got in on the act initially with conviction, trying hard to prevent it from falling victim to formula. There were some moments, however transitory they might have been, when a sense of expectations drifted in the air. Apuia’s snap shot from the distance, Manvir Singh runs and a couple of Ryan Williams’ attempts elicited roars of appreciation from the crowd. Those were the times when energy got blended with purpose in Indian players’ footsteps and embraced the possibility of matching the South American giants with a fearlessly combative mentality. On occasions when Vinicius and Pedro and others came calling with their usual attacking aspirations, they were stopped in their tracks by some well-executed offside traps from Anwar Ali and Co.However, two poor judgments allowed Brazil to make the script look familiar. When Estevao, facing a challenge from Ashique Kuruniyan, let fly a powerful left-footer, the India goalkeeper wearing the captain’s armband, couldn’t hold on to it.Soon Pedro, who replaced injured Barcelona star Raphinha in Carlos Ancelotti’s line-up, saw his header hit the post. And when the Flamengo star, who was ignored for Brazil’s World Cup squad, latched on to Estevao’s brilliant through-ball, Gurpreet was again found wanting in closing out the space and couldn’t prevent the ball from rolling into the net.It could’ve been more before the break but Vinicius couldn’t beat Gurpreet from a one-on-one situation.Khalid Jamil was forced to replace Gurpreet with Prabhsukhan Gill at the second half. Ancelotti also came out with a slew of substitutions, including one to introduce Samuel in place of Vinicius. The Flamengo attacker, a key member of Ancelotti’s rebuilding Brazil, found the target twice with the kind of precision that was enough to wow the crowd.In the end, India did exhibit some moments of resolve. But against the backdrop of this quasi-heightened setting, against a full-strength Brazil, once it got down to the business of developing into a linearity, any attempt to frame this match as a conventional David-vs-Goliath clash always looked outlandish and outmoded.
Article Summary: Brazil beat India 4-0 in their World Cup warm-up match. Samuel Lino scored twice in the second half for the hosts. India goalkeeper Gurpreet Singh Sandhu was partially responsible for allowing Brazil to go 2-0 up in the first half.

Article Title: India 0-4 Brazil: Five-time champions prove too much for Blue Tigers in historic Kolkata friendly
Article Text:
Soccer Football - International Friendly - India v Brazil - Salt Lake Stadium, Kolkata, India - October 3, 2026 Brazil players and mascot Canarinho acknowledges fans after the match REUTERS/Sahiba Chawdhary

India start boldly, and Brazil cannot find their rhythm

Soccer Football - International Friendly - India v Brazil - Salt Lake Stadium, Kolkata, India - October 3, 2026 Brazil's Vinicius Junior in action with India's Ryan Williams REUTERS/Sahiba Chawdhary

Estevao breaks the resistance, then Pedro punishes India
