Kolkata: Brazil's Pedro celebrates after scoring the team's second goal during an International friendly Football match between India and Brazil, in Kolkata. (PTI Photo/Swapan Mahapatra)(PTI10_03_2026_000667A)

Jamil changes his goalkeeper, but Lino takes over

Brazil's Gabriel Magalhães and India's Manvir Singh fight for the ball during their international friendly soccer match in Kolkata, India, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Bikas Das)

Brazil finish the job, while India get a lesson to remember

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Kolkata: Brazil's players shakes hands with India's players before an International friendly Football match between India and Brazil, in Kolkata. (PTI Photo/Swapan Mahapatra)(PTI10_03_2026_000616B)

For 27 minutes, India looked ready to make Brazil work for every inch at Salt Lake Stadium. The Blue Tigers arrived with some confidence after holding 44th-ranked Panama to a 1-1 draw, but Brazil, ranked fifth, eventually showed just how wide the gap becomes when elite quality starts finding its rhythm.The 133-place gap between India and Brazil in the FIFA rankings was impossible to ignore before kick-off, with the visitors representing the highest-ranked opposition India have faced since the world rankings were introduced in 1992.Still, Khalid Jamil’s side did not spend the opening minutes simply sitting back and admiring Brazil. India kept their defensive shape tight, tried to close the passing lanes into midfield and repeatedly looked towards Manvir Singh and Ryan Williams when possession turned over.That approach also gave India an interesting way of dealing with Vinicius Junior. Rather than constantly doubling up on the Real Madrid winger, India often left him with space on the left and trusted their defensive line to catch him offside when he tried to burst behind.Vinicius still caused problems, making several dangerous runs and forcing Gurpreet Singh Sandhu into important saves, but India largely prevented him from becoming the headline-maker Brazil needed.He was eventually substituted at half-time, having failed to find the net despite threatening repeatedly.At the other end, India were not entirely passive. For a brief spell, the crowd of around 51,000 had plenty to celebrate during those opening exchanges, especially when Ryan Williams and Manvir Singh began carrying the ball into Brazil’s half. India even won successive corners around the 27th minute, suggesting that perhaps this historic night could become a genuinely competitive contest.The breakthrough finally arrived in the 28th minute, and it came from the sort of individual quality from Estevao that makes the ranking gap feel very real.The Chelsea-bound winger received possession on the right, worked his way inside and found enough room to unleash a powerful left-footed strike towards the near post. Gurpreet got a hand to the effort, but could not keep the ball out as Brazil finally found the opening they had been searching for.India did not fold immediately, but Brazil were beginning to see more of the ball in dangerous areas. Pedro then rattled the post with a powerful header in the 36th minute, giving India another warning that their resistance was starting to crack.Six minutes later, the second goal arrived through a brilliant piece of combination play. Estevao spotted Pedro making a run behind Anwar Ali and threaded a defence-splitting pass into his path, allowing the Brazilian forward to shoot from a tight angle.Gurpreet reached the effort and appeared to have enough of it covered, but the ball squirmed underneath his palm and slowly found its way over the line. Brazil were two ahead in the 42nd minute, and India had suddenly gone from believing in an upset to facing a serious second-half challenge.Jamil reacted at half-time by making three changes, with Prabhsukhan Singh Gill replacing Gurpreet Singh Sandhu to make his senior international debut, while Mohammed Sanan and Jay Gupta also entered the game.Carlo Ancelotti went even further, making five changes of his own. Vinicius Junior was among those withdrawn, while Samuel Lino, Bruno Guimaraes and others came on as the Brazilian manager continued experimenting with his squad.India immediately showed more attacking intent. Manvir used his strength brilliantly to hold off Marquinhos in the 55th minute before squeezing a shot towards the near post, but Pedro Morisco made the save.Ryan Williams then came close in the 63rd minute after beating his man and driving into the box, only for Mauro Júnior to throw himself in front of the shot. Manvir went close again shortly afterwards, sending a rising effort wide from a narrow angleThose chances offered India a reminder that they could still hurt Brazil, but the response from the visitors was ruthless. In the 57th minute, Bijoy Varghese gave the ball away while trying to play out from the back, Brazil immediately pounced and Samuel Lino received possession on the left side of the box.Lino created the necessary space before curling a beautiful finish beyond Gill and into the bottom corner. Brazil had their third, and the contest was effectively settled.India kept making changes, with Jamil eventually sending on Mehtab Singh, Macarton Nickson, Rahim Ali, Vikram Partap Singh and Farukh Choudhary for Anwar Ali, Anirudh Thapa, Apuia, Manvir Singh and Ryan Williams.There were still flashes of promise, although India’s possession increasingly stayed in front of Brazil rather than threatening their goal. Endrick also found space behind the defence, but one promising attack ended with his shot going wide and the offside flag already raised.Brazil wanted more, and they got it deep into stoppage time. Samuel Lino navigated the space around the edge of the box, cut inside and found a gap before unleashing a low drive towards the near post.The shot was struck with such pace that it squeezed through Gill’s palm and into the net in the fifth minute of added time. Lino had his second, Brazil had their fourth and the final whistle followed almost immediately.The result was harsh on an India side that had genuinely competed during the opening half-hour, but it also provided exactly the kind of experience Jamil’s team needed from this international window.India had already taken confidence from facing Panama, a World Cup-playing side ranked 44th, before stepping up dramatically in opposition quality against Brazil.There is another heavyweight waiting immediately. India return to Salt Lake Stadium on October 6 to face Uruguay, ranked 20th in the world, giving Jamil another opportunity to test his players against a major international side.Brazil may have exposed the distance India still need to travel, but these are precisely the nights that can accelerate that learning. The Blue Tigers now have three days to absorb the lessons before another World Cup nation arrives in Kolkata.
Article Summary: Brazil beat India 2-0 at Salt Lake Stadium in Kolkata on Saturday. Estevao and Pedro scored the goals for the hosts. India are ranked 44th in the world, Brazil are fifth. India have not beaten a top-10 ranked team since 1992.

Article Title: Kolkata, AIFF pull out all stops for India vs Brazil but crowd stays away
Article Text:
Salt Lake Stadium (Photo/TimesofIndia.com)

TimesofIndia.com in Kolkata:

There were large swathes of empty seats across the Salt Lake Stadium for the India vs Brazil friendly game in Kolkata. (Image: TimesofIndia.com)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view Was the high ticket price a significant factor in the low turnout? Yes, it deterred many fans No, price was not an issue 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The All India Football Federation (AIFF) and the West Bengal government pulled out all stops to make Brazil's first-ever appearance on Indian soil a historic affair. Around 2,000 policemen were stationed at the Salt Lake Stadium on Saturday. More than 400 volunteers also chipped in. Separate companies of the central forces were also employed to keep miscreants at bay. Over a 100 temporary cameras were installed to add to the 200-plus CCTVs already in place. Yet, around an hour before the 7:30 pm kickoff, it appeared that the security were outnumbering the audience.In many ways, it was a historic occasion. Brazil hadn't faced a team as lower ranked than India in 28 years. India hadn't gone up against a team as higher ranked as Brazil since rankings were introduced in August 1993. It helps significantly that Kolkata raves over Brazil (and Argentina).When the game did kickoff, with Brazil's anthem being followed by India's, thousands more had walked in. But there were still large swathes of empty seats across the 85,000-seater stadium, of which around 65,000 are used. A massive lower block behind one of the goals remained largely empty.As did a big section parallel to the dugouts. The official attendance blared as an announcement was 51,402. By most local accounts, that was touted as an inflated number.The AIFF had reportedly spent over Rs 50 crore to bring Brazil, Uruguay and Panama to this part of the world. An additional, Rs 6 crore had been shelled out for a charter flight to fly in the 90-member Brazilian contingent from Australia. To recover those costs, ticket prices had been kept high. In the same vein, tickets were offered at a discount to members of the local clubs: East Bengal, Mohun Bagan and Mohammedan Sporting. With situation still not getting better ahead of the marquee contest, a buy-one-get-one offer was also floated.The fact that this fixture came two weeks before Durga Puja kept families away."The reason that people have stayed away is that Durga Puja is coming up. Had this fixture taken place during the winter, the sale would have been much higher. Football is a religion, a festival for Bengalis but Durga Puja is even bigger. And families end up spending a lot of money during the festival so people have stayed away now," said a youth donning the colours of Mohun Bagan outside the Salt Lake Stadium."If the same Brazil had come during the winter or even after Durga Puja, people would have come. You would have been desperate to get a single ticket. Price is not a big issue in my opinion. Even when Lionel Messi came, and didn't play, people had spent money for his visit. India vs Bangladesh here had also attracted 63,000 people. So Durga Buja is the main reason people have kept away," he continued.Some metres away, a flag and scarves seller occupied the street near the iconic stadium. The India and Brazil jerseys went for Rs 350 each, as he vouched for their quality. With tifos and banners not allowed inside, mini scarves worth Rs 200 were being sold instead. The seller begrudged the activity despite the magnitude of the occasion."Had Neymar been here, things would have been bigger. Unfortunately, there is no Neymar, no big name, so fewer people have come," he said disappointingly.
Article Summary: The All India Football Federation (AIFF) and the West Bengal government pulled out all stops to make Brazil's first-ever appearance on Indian soil a historic affair. The AIFF had reportedly spent over Rs 50 crore to bring Brazil, Uruguay and Panama to this part of the world. To recover those costs, ticket prices had been kept high.

Article Title: Ronaldo likes video slamming his ‘grotesque’ treatment by Portugal compared with Messi in Argentina
Article Text:
FILE - Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo waves following the World Cup Group K soccer match between Colombia and Portugal in Miami Gardens, Fla., Saturday, June 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell, file)

Ronaldo appears to endorse Felipe Melo's criticism

Ronaldo appeared to like Felipe Melo’s video calling Portugal’s treatment of him “grotesque” compared with Messi’s in Argentina.

Ronaldo left Portugal after Jesus press conference

Portugal face Norway again without Ronaldo

Cristiano Ronaldo has appeared to send a pointed message over his Portugal exit without saying a word. The Al Nassr star appeared to like a video in which former Brazil international Felipe Melo accused Portuguese football of treating Ronaldo far worse than Argentina has treated Lionel Messi, adding fresh fuel to the controversy surrounding his departure from the national team and his strained relationship with Jorge Jesus.Ronaldo's Instagram activity has added another layer to the controversy after the Al Nassr forward appeared to like a video in which former Brazil international Felipe Melo criticised the way the Portuguese star has been treated by his national team.Melo drew a direct comparison between the treatment of Ronaldo by Portuguese football and the way Argentina has embraced Lionel Messi, arguing that there has been a noticeably different level of respect surrounding the two legendary forwards.“There is a grotesque difference in the way the Portuguese treat Cristiano Ronaldo and the way the Argentines treat Lionel Messi,” Melo said.“I see much more respect from opponents when they play against Cristiano Ronaldo. Yesterday, Højlund got very upset with Jorge Jesus because his idol is Cristiano. It’s wrong ... nobody comes close to Cristiano Ronaldo. You can’t let him leave like nothing happened,” Melo continued.The comments quickly gained traction on social media, with the video receiving more than 250,000 likes after being published on Friday night.Ronaldo's account was among those that appeared to have liked the post, although it remains unclear whether Ronaldo personally made the interaction himself. The apparent endorsement has nevertheless attracted considerable attention because Melo's argument closely reflects the wider discussion surrounding Ronaldo's abrupt departure from the Portugal camp.Melo had also referenced Rasmus Højlund's reaction following Denmark's 4–2 defeat by Portugal, after the Danish striker appeared to have an uncomfortable exchange with Jesus at the final whistle.Højlund had earlier celebrated his goal by performing Ronaldo's trademark “Siuuu” celebration, explaining afterwards that he had used it as a tribute to his childhood idol rather than as a provocation towards Portugal.The controversy began after Ronaldo was left on the bench during Portugal's 2–1 Nations League victory over Norway, with the forward warming up for around 20 to 30 minutes before Jesus ultimately decided against sending him onto the pitch.Jesus subsequently insisted that there had been no incident between himself and Ronaldo, explaining that he had told the veteran forward he would consider bringing him on during the second half before eventually choosing another approach.Ronaldo left the Portugal national team camp following a press conference held by Jesus, later confirming his decision through a statement posted on Instagram.“After the press conference of the National Team coach, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I decided to leave the National Team camp,” Ronaldo wrote.“In due time, I will tell all the Portuguese about the reasons that motivated my departure from the national team, which I always dedicated myself to.”“Now it's time to wish good luck to Portugal and all my teammates, without exception.”Ronaldo has not publicly provided any further explanation since that statement, although his friend and El Chiringuito reporter Edu Aguirre has claimed that the forward felt “betrayed” after Jesus allegedly promised to publicly acknowledge his decision to leave Ronaldo on the bench against Norway and apologise for the way the situation had unfolded.According to Aguirre, Jesus had told Ronaldo that he would address the decision during his next press conference and acknowledge that he had made a mistake by not bringing the veteran forward onto the pitch after allowing him to warm up for around 20 to 30 minutes. Jesus ultimately did not make that apology or publicly acknowledge the decision in the way Ronaldo had reportedly been promised, and Aguirre said that this contributed to Ronaldo deciding to leave the national team camp.Ronaldo's sister, Elma dos Santos Aveiro, has also criticised the situation publicly, taking aim at the organisation surrounding the Portuguese national team while defending her brother's standing within the country's football history.“The national team deserved better structuring. The Portuguese press deserved more competence and fewer guesses,” she wrote on Instagram.“As for the Portuguese... well, they don't deserve the best in anything. We are envious, contemptuous, ignorant, and we deserve to return to the mediocrity we always had in football before CR7. Thank you for everything CR7!”Portugal have attempted to move forward with their Nations League campaign despite the controversy, with Jesus' side winning all three of their matches during the current international window against Wales, Norway and Denmark.Their next assignment comes on Sunday at the Estádio do Dragão in Porto, where Portugal will face Norway and Erling Haaland as they look to close the FIFA international window with another result.The match will be played without Ronaldo after his departure from the squad, leaving Jesus to manage the team while attention continues to surround the circumstances of the veteran forward's exit.Portugal's recent run includes a 2–1 victory over Norway, the match in which Ronaldo remained an unused substitute despite warming up during the second half.That decision was followed by Jesus' press conference, Ronaldo's departure and the subsequent public debate over whether the forward was treated appropriately by his national team.The apparent Instagram endorsement of Melo's criticism has now added another element to that dispute, particularly because Ronaldo himself has so far limited his public comments to the statement confirming his departure and the promise that he will explain the reasons for it “in due time”.
Article Summary: Cristiano Ronaldo appears to endorse Felipe Melo's criticism of Portugal. The Al Nassr star appeared to like a video in which former Brazil international Melo criticised the way the Portuguese star has been treated by his national team. Melo drew a direct comparison between the treatment of Ronaldo by Portuguese football and the way Argentina has embraced Lionel Messi.
